item.title: Govt appoints Mathew, Sinha, Akbaruddin as part-time RBI board directors
item.description: Annie George Mathew, Janmejaya Sinha and Syed Akbaruddin have been appointed part-time, non-official directors on the RBI's central board for four-year terms ...
item.dc:creator: BS Reporter
item.content:encoded: The central government has appointed former bureaucrat Annie George Mathew, economist Janmejaya Sinha and former diplomat Syed Akbaruddin as part-time, non-official directors on the Central Board of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for a four-year term effective from August 24, 2026, the central bank said on Monday. The current strength of the board is 14, including the governor and deputy governors, apart from Anuradha Thakur, secretary, Department of Economic Affairs, and Sanjay Lohiya, secretary, Department of Financial Services (DFS). The other members include Revathy Iyer and Sachin Chaturvedi. Last week, the government appointed former ISRO Chairman Somnath S and reappointed Anand Mahindra, chairman, Mahindra Group, to the central board. Mathew is a former special secretary in the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance, and is also a full-time member of the Sixteenth Finance Commission. She is an officer of the Indian Audit and Accounts Service and has over 30 years of experience in public finance, financial management, government audit and accounts. Janmejaya Sinha is an economist and management consultant. He is chairman, Boston Consulting Group (BCG) India, and has also served as chairman of BCG Asia-Pacific. He has also been part of several regulatory committees. Akbaruddin is a former Permanent Representative of India to the United Nations and a former spokesperson for the Ministry of External Affairs. He is currently serving as the dean of the Kautilya School of Public Policy in Hyderabad. Some of the members whose terms ended this year included Satish Marathe, Swaminathan Gurumurthy, Venu Srinivasan, Pankaj Ramanbhai Patel and Ravindra H. Dholakia, apart from the government officials. The government had renominated Revathy Iyer and Sachin Chaturvedi as part-time, non-official directors on the Central Board of the Reserve Bank of India on September 18, 2022, for a period of four years.

item.title: SBI flags 'chalk and cheese' divide in RBI's monetary policy signals
item.description: SBI Research says the MPC minutes carried a more hawkish tone than the RBI governor's remarks, leaving markets uncertain about the future course of interest rates ...
item.dc:creator: Anjali Kumari
item.content:encoded: The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) recent policy communications have sent conflicting signals on the future course of interest rates, according to the latest report by the State Bank of India (SBI).   The report compared the minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee’s (MPC’s) August meeting, the accompanying monetary policy statement, and RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra’s public remarks, and found the three documents diverging in tone. Soumya Kanti Ghosh, group chief economic adviser at the bank, noted that the MPC minutes carried a distinctly hawkish undertone, dwelling on inflation risks and keeping the door open for further rate action. “The recent monetary policy minutes, monetary policy press statement and the governor’s statement for August and even earlier months reveal the conundrum of ‘chalk and cheese’ in monetary policy. There were clear yet divergent signals from these three statements despite originating from the same institution/source,” Ghosh said while noting a “communication puzzle” emerging from the RBI’s latest policy cycle. The governor’s statement, by comparison, struck a calmer, more data-dependent note, giving more weight to the growth momentum and financial-sector conditions than to inflation risk. To capture this gap, the bank has built a tone index using the governor’s statement as a baseline of 1. On that scale, the MPC minutes scored 1.76 in June and 1.82 in August (a reading more than 1 signalling greater hawkishness). The widest gaps between the two showed up specifically in discussions of rates and the policy stance, and in the treatment of inflation, the report said. That split, according to the report, has left markets guessing whether to price in a rate increase in October or to take the governor’s cautious tone as the guide to the regulator’s next move. SBI Research said the window for an increase had technically opened but that the decision remained delicately poised, pointing to two broad sources of uncertainty. The MPC kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent for the fourth meeting in a row while maintaining the “neutral” stance. On the external front, the report flagged resilient but fragile growth in the United States (US), buoyed by consumer spending and artificial intelligence-related investment, but shadowed by a surprise contraction in non-farm payrolls and a national debt, which has now crossed $40 trillion. It noted that the US Treasury’s decision to at least double its bond buyback size made a near-term rate increase in the US look unlikely even as the move raised the prospects of the Fed eventually stepping in with more direct intervention. The report pointed to an uneven and underwhelming monsoon in India as a bigger worry. Despite an overall shortfall of only around 13 per cent, key foodgrain-producing states such as Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and Karnataka are running large deficits, and forecaster Skymet has since cut its seasonal outlook and raised the probability of drought conditions. Against this backdrop, the report has argued that addressing rural distress, including through the newly launched rural employment-guarantee scheme, which has so far seen a sharp fall in person-days generated compared with its predecessor, should take precedence over tightening monetary policy. Pursuing an expansionary push in rural spending alongside a rate increase, the report cautioned, would be difficult to reconcile.

item.title: Caution over Trump's unpredictable behaviour led India to skip full presser
item.description: The clarification came after US envoy Sergio Gor publicly revealed that New Delhi had communicated to the US side to skip taking questions by the two leaders.
item.content:encoded:
Home / India News / Caution over Trump's unpredictable behaviour led India to skip full presser

Caution over Trump's unpredictable behaviour led India to skip full presser The clarification came after US envoy Sergio Gor publicly revealed that New Delhi had communicated to the US side to skip taking questions by the two leaders.

US President Donald Trump (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Aug 24 2026 | 11:08 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Concerns over US President Donald Trump's "unpredictable behaviour" towards many foreign leaders led the Indian side to opt against a full press conference by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the American leader following their talks in France in June, government sources said on Monday.

The clarification came after US envoy Sergio Gor publicly revealed that New Delhi had communicated to the US side to skip taking questions by the two leaders.

The sources emphasised that discussions regarding leaders' public appearances are standard protocol and part of routine diplomatic practice.

Modi and Trump held bilateral talks on June 17 in Evian-les-Bains on the sidelines of the G7 summit. The meeting was widely viewed as a step forward in mending bilateral ties, which had faced severe strain over the preceding year.

The fresh controversy comes amid a growing perception of a lack of intensity in overall relations between the two sides, with the much-talked-about bilateral trade deal remaining in limbo. Also Read

Trump threatens 50% tariffs on all cars, trucks from Canada amid trade spat

Trump administration moves to impose over $100K fee on H-1B worker visas

'Standard protocol': Govt sources on US envoy's remark on media interaction

Defiant Iran says new sanctions threatened by 'desperate' US will fail

PM urges space startups to make India global hub for talent, innovation

The sources said that foreign delegations meeting the US President are "wary about his unpredictable behaviour as may be seen from his interactions with the presidents of South Africa and Ukraine".

"Thus, the cautious approach by India," said one of them.

The sources said discussions regarding arrangements for public appearances of leaders ahead of any VVIP visit are normal practice.

"In this regard, the Indian side communicated its standard practice for such visits," one of the sources said.

In the course of an interactive session at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum late last week, Gor highlighted the "deep and personal friendship" between Trump and Modi and said the equation between the two leaders makes his job easier.

The envoy then brought up the meeting between the two leaders in France.

"We were behind the stage, and at one point, it was just the President and I. And he asked me, 'What are the Indians going to raise?' We went over some topics and he said 'do they have any asks'," Gor said.

"MEA had one ask and it was let's bring in the media, let's not do a full press conference, no questions." Gor said he told Trump that the "Indians prefer no questions...He (Trump) said, 'Sure, no problem'".

The envoy said when the meeting started, the media entered with some 50 cameras, adding Modi and Trump spoke for a few minutes.

"As soon as they get done, the first thing the President does, he looks up at the cameras and asks, 'Any questions?'" he said.

"And that opened everything up," he added.

The US envoy suggested that Trump had forgotten the request from the Indian side and ended up taking many questions from the media.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: Stock Market Close: Sensex sheds 172 pts; Nifty settles at 24,219; Nifty PSU Bank tumbles 1%
item.description: The GIFT Nifty signalled a positive open for the Nifty50 as investors await US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's announcement of Iran sanctions ...
item.dc:creator: SI Reporter
item.content:encoded: Stock Market Highlights on Monday, Aug 24, 2026: The benchmark indices settled on a negative note as geopolitical tension increased after Iran threatened to seize vessels and change transit rules for the Strait of Hormuz ahead of the US’s announcement of sanctions against Iran.   The Sensex fell 171.72 points or 0.22 per cent to 77,369.11 and the Nifty50 was down 32.95 points or 0.14 per cent at 24,219.05.  SBI Life Insurance Company, Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone, and Bajaj Finance were the top losers in the Nifty50 index.   In the broader markets, the Nifty MidCap rose 0.13 per cent and the Nifty SmallCap fell 0.26 per cent. Sector-wise, the Nifty PSU Bank declined the most, while the Nifty Metal outperformed.
